summary: Niklas Nielsen, CTO and co-founder of log10, presents llmeval, a command-line tool designed to help teams ship reliable LLM products by enabling systematic evaluation of generative AI applications. Nielsen frames the core problem: the industry has rapidly deployed GPT-based features but now faces a 'now what' moment because without clear definitions of quality in generative settings, evolving applications through prompt changes, model provider switches, self-hosting, or fine-tuning is risky. llmeval initializes a folder structure for storing prompts and tests, built on Meta's Hydra configuration system for extensibility. Metrics are implemented in Python and can invoke LLMs or any custom logic. The tool supports flexible test criteria, acknowledging that fuzzy model outputs rarely guarantee binary pass/fail; instead, criteria like 'three out of five should pass' are supported. By default, five samples are run per test for stability, configurable via llmeval.yaml. Nielsen demonstrates a math test where a prompt asks the model to add four and five and return only the answer. When prompt engineering constraints are removed, GPT-3.5 and Claude produce verbose, failing outputs. Reinstating constraints fixes results. The tool generates per-run and overall summary reports. A second demonstration covers tool use—Python code generation—where additional prompt clauses ensure parseable output. Nielsen also introduces model-based evaluation, where a larger model grades outputs from other LLMs on scales such as 1 to 5. He notes pitfalls including models preferring their own output and difficulty with calibrated point scores. To address these, log10 bridges model-based and human feedback by modeling individual reviewers' feedback patterns, creating an AI reviewer that mimics a specific human's grading style, and providing AI-suggested answers for pending human feedback.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

Default behavior runs five samples per test for stability, but all settings are configurable via llmeval.yaml
Reports provide per-run summaries and overall views, supporting flexible pass criteria like 3 out of 5 should pass
Prompt engineering matters: removing constraints like 'only return the answer' causes GPT-3.5 and Claude to produce verbose, failing outputs
Model-based evaluation uses larger models as judges but suffers from self-preference bias and poor point-score calibration
log10 bridges human and model feedback by creating AI models that mimic specific human reviewers' feedback patterns (e.g., 'auto John')

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Nielsen introduces himself as CTO and co-founder of log10 and frames the problem: the industry has rapidly deployed GPT-based features but faces a 'now what' moment because without knowing what good means in a generative setting, evolving applications is risky and hard.

sections.title: llmeval Tool Introduction
sections.summary: Introduces llmeval as a command-line tool that creates a folder structure for prompts and tests, built on Meta's Hydra configuration system. Metrics are in Python and can call out to LLMs. The tool generates reports and supports flexible test criteria like 3 out of 5 passing, since model outputs are fuzzy.

sections.title: Demo Setup - Math Test
sections.summary: Demonstrates creating a directory, virtual environment, installing llmeval, and initializing the folder structure. Shows a math prompt template ('what is a plus b, only return the answer') and a test comparing actual output to expected, with a metric and pass/fail result. Notes Claude prepends spaces that must be stripped.

sections.title: Running Tests and Reports
sections.summary: Runs the math test across Claude, GPT-4, and GPT-3.5. Removing prompt engineering constraints causes GPT-3.5 and Claude to become chatty and fail. Reinstating constraints fixes results. Reports show per-run summaries and overall status. Default is 5 samples; configurable via llmeval.yaml.

sections.title: Tool Use - Python Code Generation
sections.summary: Demonstrates a tool-use test generating Python code, where additional prompt clauses ensure only parseable Python is returned without surrounding explanations. Tests pass, confirming the tool-use evaluation works.

sections.title: Model-Based Evaluation
sections.summary: Introduces model-based evaluation where a larger model grades or judges output from another LLM, enabling nuanced scoring (pass/fail, 1-5, preferences). Notes pitfalls: self-preference bias, poor point-score calibration. Mentions work on increasing feedback accuracy.

sections.title: Human-Model Feedback Bridging and Conclusion
sections.summary: Describes bridging model-based and human feedback by modeling individual reviewers' patterns (e.g., 'auto John') to generate AI feedback for incoming completions. Shows AI-suggested answers for pending human feedback. Concludes with documentation links and contact information.

demonstrations: Math test: adding 4+5 with prompt requiring answer-only output across Claude, GPT-4, and GPT-3.5

limitations: Model-based evaluation has self-preference bias when models judge their own outputs
Models are not very good at giving calibrated point scores (0-1 or 0-100)
Setting up tests and gathering test cases takes a considerable amount of work
Fuzzy model outputs rarely guarantee binary pass/fail outcomes
Some models like Claude prepend spaces that can affect string comparisons
